findings.title: Hello Again: Exploiting Replay Protected Monotonic Counters to Brute-Force Windows Hello PINs
findings.summary_md: Technische Universität Berlin researchers submitted the Hello Again paper on November 13, describing the first practical security analysis of Replay Protected Monotonic Counters in shipping x86 systems. They show that AMD's NV controller does not verify RPMC increments, allowing an interposer to suppress them unnoticed, and that Winbond SPI flash leaks its HMAC key under voltage glitching. On two AMD desktops without RPMC flash, reflashing an older image reset the firmware TPM lockout counters. On locked, encrypted hardware they recovered a four-digit Windows Hello PIN in 40 hours instead of 69 days and reduced the worst case for a default six-digit BitLocker TPM+PIN from 19 years to 20 days.

findings.title: Hello Again: Exploiting Replay Protected Monotonic Counters to Brute-Force Windows Hello PINs
findings.summary_md: The BIFOLD research institute listed the Hello Again paper on November 13, 2026, noting that it received a Distinguished Paper Award at ACM CCS 2026. The page reproduces the abstract, which describes low-cost interposer hardware, an RPMC increment suppression flaw in AMD's NV controller, and an HMAC key leak in Winbond flash under voltage glitching. It states that a recovered PIN also grants access to device-bound keys and Hello-based enterprise SSO.

findings.title: INTEL-2026-11-16-001-HelloAgain
findings.summary_md: Intel published announcement 2026-11-16-001 in response to the Technische Universität Berlin Hello Again paper. Intel's public bulletin listing dates the announcement to November 16, 2026. Contemporaneous reporting quoting the notice says Intel places the weakness in third-party flash, states that the research did not demonstrate a vulnerability in an Intel component, and directs customers to ask their PC manufacturer whether an update exists.

findings.title: Replay Protected Monotonic Counters (RPMC) Increment Suppression Vulnerability
findings.summary_md: AMD published bulletin AMD-SB-7079 on November 17, 2026, for CVE-2026-43613, scored CVSS 4.0 5.1 with physical access required. The bulletin says insufficient authentication of RPMC increment completion in the Secure Processor firmware can let a physically present attacker suppress counter updates through an interposer and bypass rollback protection on systems with RPMC-capable SPI flash. AMD recommends maintaining physical control and watching for tampering until firmware is available, and lists target releases including ComboAM5PI_1.2.0.3n for EPYC 4004 and ComboAM4v2PI_1.2.0.13 RC1 for EPYC 4005 in November 2026, with embedded lines targeted for February 2027.
